topics.title: Agricultural Practices
objectives: Student can define crop and classify crops into Kharif and Rabi categories based on the season of sowing
Student can list the seven basic agricultural practices in their chronological order of execution
visualIdeas: A timeline showing the calendar months of Kharif (June to October) and Rabi (November to April) with icons of maize and wheat respectively
A sequential list with modern icons representing each step of crop production from soil preparation to storage

topics.title: Basic Practices of Crop Production
objectives: Student can explain why certain crops cannot be grown in the winter season
Student can outline the overall requirement of continuous water, nutrients, and soil upkeep for crop survival
visualIdeas: An illustration of a paddy field flooded with water, contrasted with dry cracked soil, to show why paddy requires specific monsoon seasons

topics.title: Preparation of Soil
objectives: Student can explain why loosening and turning the soil is necessary for root respiration, water absorption, and earthworm growth
Student can identify agricultural implements like the plough, hoe, and tractor-driven cultivator from diagrams
visualIdeas: A close-up diagram showing earthworms in porous, loosened soil with arrows pointing to the roots of a plant representing air passage
A split-screen drawing comparing a traditional wooden plough drawn by bulls with a modern tractor-mounted cultivator

topics.title: Sowing
objectives: Student can explain the water flotation method of separating healthy seeds from damaged ones
Student can compare the traditional funnel-shaped sowing tool with a modern seed drill in terms of spacing, depth, and protection from birds
visualIdeas: An animation showing damaged hollow seeds floating on water while healthy dense seeds sink to the bottom of a beaker
A diagram of a seed drill showing the funnel, tubes, and seed placement at uniform depth inside the soil furrow

topics.title: Adding Manure and Fertilizers
objectives: Student can define manure and fertilizers and list three differences between them
Student can explain the process of crop rotation and state how it naturally replenishes soil nitrogen
visualIdeas: A comparison table detailing the organic nature and humus contribution of manure versus chemical fertilizers like urea, NPK, and superphosphate
A crop rotation cycle diagram alternating between a legume crop (with root nodules) and a cereal crop

topics.title: Irrigation
objectives: Student can define irrigation and list traditional methods of water supply
Student can describe the working mechanisms of modern water-saving irrigation systems: sprinkler and drip irrigation
visualIdeas: Schematic diagrams of a sprinkler system showing a central pump, main pipe, lateral pipes, and rotating nozzles spraying water
A close-up diagram of a drip irrigation pipe delivering water drops directly at the base or root zone of a plant

topics.title: Protection from Weeds
objectives: Student can define weeds and explain their competitive effect on crop plants for light, space, and nutrients
Student can list methods of weeding, including manual removal, tilling, and chemical weedicides like 2,4-D
visualIdeas: A diagram showing a crop plant crowded by weeds, with arrows showing competing demands for sunlight, water, and minerals
An illustration of a farmer wearing a protective mask spraying weedicide selectively on wild grass between crops

topics.title: Harvesting
objectives: Student can define harvesting, threshing, and winnowing
Student can identify the dual role of a 'Combine' machine in harvesting and threshing
visualIdeas: An illustration of a combine harvester with labels pointing to the cutting assembly and the grain-separating drum
A diagram showing the process of winnowing where grain falls vertically while lighter chaff is blown away by the wind

topics.title: Storage
objectives: Student can state the preventive measures required before storing grains to protect them from moisture, insects, and microorganisms
Student can differentiate between domestic storage using dried neem leaves and large-scale storage in silos and granaries
visualIdeas: A cross-section of a tall steel silo showing aeration vents and grain level indicators
A contrast drawing of a dry, well-ventilated granary with neatly stacked gunny bags versus a moldy wet pile showing fungal growth

topics.title: Food from Animals
objectives: Student can define animal husbandry
Student can list food products obtained from animals along with their main nutritional benefits
visualIdeas: A mind map with 'Animal Husbandry' at the center, branching into dairy, poultry, and fish culture, listing major products and nutrients

topics.title: Microorganisms
objectives: Student can classify microorganisms into four major groups: bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and algae
Student can describe the unique characteristics of viruses that distinguish them from other living organisms
visualIdeas: A grid layout showing sketches of Chlamydomonas, Amoeba, Penicillium, and rod-shaped bacteria
A diagram of a bacteriophage virus showing its protein coat and inner genetic material, with an arrow indicating host cell entry

topics.title: Where do Microorganisms Live?
objectives: Student can identify the diverse environments, ranging from ice-cold climates to hot springs, where microorganisms survive
Student can explain how single-celled versus multicellular microorganisms differ in their living patterns (isolated vs. colonial)
visualIdeas: An Earth landscape scene highlighting extreme habitats (hot springs, desert sand, polar ice, deep ocean) where microbes are found

topics.title: Friendly Microorganisms
objectives: Student can describe the role of Lactobacillus in converting milk to curd
Student can explain the process of fermentation in bread making and alcohol production by yeast
Student can define antibiotics and describe how a vaccine helps the body build antibodies
visualIdeas: A step-by-step cartoon of yeast cells undergoing budding, releasing carbon dioxide bubbles to make dough rise
A timeline of memory cells forming after a weakened pathogen (vaccine) is introduced to the body

topics.title: Harmful Microorganisms
objectives: Student can identify common plant and animal diseases caused by pathogens (e.g., Citrus canker, Rust of wheat, Anthrax)
Student can list carriers of disease-causing microbes like the female Anopheles mosquito and the housefly
visualIdeas: A table matching pathogens (bacteria, fungi, virus) with their respective plant and human diseases and mode of transmission
An illustration of a housefly sitting on refuse and then on uncovered food, showing mechanical transfer of pathogens

topics.title: Food Preservation
objectives: Student can list five common methods of food preservation including salting, sugaring, oil/vinegar, and pasteurization
Student can explain the mechanism of pasteurization of milk in terms of heating temperature and rapid cooling
visualIdeas: A schematic of a milk pasteurizer heating milk to 70 degrees Celsius for 15-30 seconds, followed by a blue arrow showing sudden chilling
A visual guide of different preserved items (pickles in oil, jam in heavy sugar syrup, salted fish) with labels explaining how water activity is lowered

topics.title: Nitrogen Fixation
objectives: Student can identify the symbiotic relationship between Rhizobium bacteria and the root nodules of leguminous plants
Student can state the role of lightning in atmospheric nitrogen fixation
visualIdeas: A close-up drawing of a leguminous root system showing pinkish nodules containing Rhizobium bacteria

topics.title: Nitrogen Cycle
objectives: Student can trace the path of nitrogen from the atmosphere through soil, plants, animals, and back to the atmosphere
Student can explain the role of denitrifying bacteria in maintaining a constant percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere
visualIdeas: A comprehensive nitrogen cycle flow diagram showing lightning, nitrogen-fixing bacteria, ammonia/nitrate conversion in soil, plant uptake, animal consumption, and denitrifying bacteria releasing N2

topics.title: Coal
objectives: Student can define carbonisation as the slow process of conversion of dead vegetation into coal
Student can state the uses of coke, coal tar, and coal gas obtained by processing coal
visualIdeas: A geological cross-section diagram showing layers of ancient swamp forest buried under high pressure and temperature turning into coal
A branching tree diagram of Coal products: Coke (reductant in metallurgy), Coal Tar (synthetic dyes/perfumes), and Coal Gas (fuel)

topics.title: Petroleum
objectives: Student can describe the formation of petroleum and natural gas from organisms living in the sea
Student can explain the process of fractional distillation used in refining petroleum to obtain products like petrol, kerosene, and diesel
visualIdeas: A diagram of an oil trap showing underground layers of water, oil, and gas beneath an impervious rock cap with a drilling rig
A simplified fractionating column showing different temperature zones and corresponding products collected at each level

topics.title: Natural Gas
objectives: Student can list the advantages of using Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) as a cleaner fuel
Student can explain why natural gas is transported through pipes over long distances
visualIdeas: A comparison chart of emissions (soot, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide) from burning coal vs. burning CNG

topics.title: Some Natural Resources are Limited
objectives: Student can explain why fossil fuels are exhaustible resources based on their formation time
Student can state key guidelines recommended by the Petroleum Conservation Research Association (PCRA) to save petrol/diesel while driving
visualIdeas: An hourglass visual representing millions of years to form fossil fuels versus seconds to burn them
A set of cartoon panels showing PCRA tips: driving at constant speed, switching off engine at traffic lights, and maintaining correct tyre pressure

topics.title: What is Combustion?
objectives: Student can define combustion as a chemical process in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give off heat
Student can define ignition temperature and explain why a substance does not catch fire if its temperature is below this limit
Student can identify inflammable substances based on their low ignition temperature
visualIdeas: An experiment showing a paper cup with water being heated over a candle flame without burning, contrasted with an empty paper cup catching fire immediately
A molecular cartoon of fuel molecules reacting with oxygen molecules to release carbon dioxide, water vapor, and energy sparks

topics.title: How Do We Control Fire?
objectives: Student can list the three essential requirements for producing fire (fuel, air, heat)
Student can explain how carbon dioxide acts as an effective fire extinguisher by cutting off the oxygen supply and cooling the fuel
visualIdeas: A fire triangle showing 'Fuel', 'Oxygen', and 'Heat' at the vertices, with an eraser crossing out one vertex to show how extinction works
A cross-section of a chemical fire extinguisher showing the cylinder, plunger, and the carbon dioxide blanket smothering a fire

topics.title: Types of Combustion
objectives: Student can classify combustion into rapid, spontaneous, and explosion with real-world examples
Student can compare spontaneous combustion of phosphorus with the explosion of a firecracker
visualIdeas: Three illustrative panels: a gas stove burner igniting instantly (rapid), a piece of white phosphorus catching fire on its own at room temperature (spontaneous), and a firecracker bursting with sound, heat, and gas release (explosion)

topics.title: Flame
objectives: Student can identify which substances produce a flame during combustion based on their ability to vaporize
Student can compare a candle flame, an LPG burner flame, and a kerosene lamp flame
visualIdeas: An illustration showing vaporizing wax rising from a candle wick to form a flame, contrasted with glowing charcoal which does not vaporize or produce a flame

topics.title: Structure of a Flame
objectives: Student can draw and label the three distinct zones of a candle flame: outer zone of complete combustion, middle zone of partial combustion, and innermost zone of unburnt wax vapours
Student can correlate the color of each zone with its temperature (blue - hottest, yellow - moderately hot, black - least hot)
visualIdeas: A detailed, large diagram of a candle flame with color coding: blue outer envelope, yellow middle mantle, black inner core around the wick
A demonstration drawing showing a glass tube inserted into the dark zone of a flame, conducting unburnt wax vapors to ignite at the other end

topics.title: What is a Fuel?
objectives: Student can list characteristics of a good/ideal fuel
Student can classify common fuels into solid, liquid, and gaseous states
visualIdeas: A checklist comparing wood, kerosene, and natural gas against 'ideal fuel' criteria (cheap, readily available, high heat value, clean-burning)

topics.title: Fuel Efficiency
objectives: Student can define calorific value of a fuel and state its unit as kilojoules per kg (kJ/kg)
Student can explain the environmental hazards of burning fuels, including acid rain, carbon monoxide poisoning, and global warming
visualIdeas: A bar chart comparing the calorific values of various fuels like cow dung cake, coal, petrol, CNG, and hydrogen
A sequence map showing sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides rising from factories, combining with clouds, and falling as acid rain onto trees and buildings

topics.title: Deforestation and Its Causes
objectives: Student can list the natural and man-made causes of deforestation
Student can identify industrialization, agriculture, forest fires, and droughts as key drivers of forest loss
visualIdeas: A split illustration showing a lush forest on one side and a cleared land with tree stumps, factories, and agricultural fields on the other

topics.title: Consequences of Deforestation
objectives: Student can explain how deforestation leads to global warming by increasing carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere
Student can describe desertification in terms of soil erosion, loss of humus, and changes in soil properties
visualIdeas: A diagram showing trees absorbing CO2 (photosynthesis) vs. a deforested land where CO2 accumulates in the atmosphere, trapping heat
A sequence showing soil erosion: rain washing away topsoil on barren land, leading to exposed rocky layers beneath

topics.title: Conservation of Forest and Wildlife
objectives: Student can define biosphere reserves, national parks, and wildlife sanctuaries
Student can compare the degree of protection and permissible human activities in protected areas vs. general areas
visualIdeas: A concentric rings diagram showing different zones of conservation, with labels explaining protected areas

topics.title: Biosphere Reserve
objectives: Student can describe the structure of a biosphere reserve including its role in conserving biodiversity and tribal culture
Student can identify the components of the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve
visualIdeas: A map layout of Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve showing Satpura National Park and Bori and Pachmarhi Sanctuaries nested within it

topics.title: Flora and Fauna
objectives: Student can define flora and fauna with local examples from a protected area
Student can list representative flora (e.g., sal, teak, wild mango) and fauna (e.g., chinkara, blue-bull, leopard) of the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve
visualIdeas: A pictorial collage separating plant species (Flora) and animal species (Fauna) with scientific or common name labels

topics.title: Endemic Species
objectives: Student can define endemic species as those found exclusively in a particular area
Student can name examples of endemic flora and fauna (e.g., giant squirrel, wild mango) of the Pachmarhi area
visualIdeas: A spotlight map highlighting an isolated geographic area with a drawing of the Indian Giant Squirrel showing it exists nowhere else

topics.title: Wildlife Sanctuary
objectives: Student can explain the primary purpose of a wildlife sanctuary as providing protection and suitable living conditions to wild animals
Student can state how poaching and capturing of animals are strictly prohibited and punishable by law
visualIdeas: A sketch of a tranquil forest landscape with deer and birds roaming freely, with a 'No Hunting' sign posted clearly at the boundary

topics.title: National Park
objectives: Student can define national parks as reserves large enough to protect entire ecosystems including flora, fauna, landscape, and historic objects
Student can describe Project Tiger and its objective in ensuring the survival and maintenance of the tiger population
visualIdeas: An illustration of a tiger in Satpura National Park, along with symbols representing rock shelters and prehistoric paintings protected inside the park

topics.title: Red Data Book
objectives: Student can define the Red Data Book and state its purpose in keeping a record of endangered species
Student can explain the difference between extinct and endangered species
visualIdeas: A catalog-style illustration labeled 'Red Data Book' with pages showing profiles of endangered animals like the red panda or tiger with their threat status

topics.title: Migration
objectives: Student can define migration as the seasonal movement of animals or birds to escape inhospitable climates or for breeding
Student can identify the Siberian crane as a migratory bird that visits India annually
visualIdeas: A map of the globe showing a dotted arrow path from cold Siberia to warm wetland sanctuaries in India with flying birds illustrated overhead

topics.title: Recycling of Paper
objectives: Student can explain why saving and recycling paper is crucial for conserving trees, energy, and water
Student can calculate the number of trees saved if paper is recycled up to 5 to 7 times
visualIdeas: A circular loop diagram showing: wood pulp -> paper production -> usage -> recycling -> new paper, highlighting the bypass of cutting fresh trees

topics.title: Reforestation
objectives: Student can define reforestation as the stocking of destroyed forests by planting new trees
Student can compare reforestation with natural afforestation
visualIdeas: A step-by-step cartoon showing children planting saplings of the same species originally present in the forest, leading to a restored forest ecosystem years later

topics.title: Modes of Reproduction
objectives: Student can classify animal reproduction into sexual and asexual modes
Student can compare the basic differences in parental involvement between sexual and asexual reproduction
visualIdeas: A simple flow diagram splitting 'Reproduction' into 'Sexual (two parents, fusion of gametes)' and 'Asexual (single parent, no gamete fusion)'

topics.title: Sexual Reproduction
objectives: Student can identify and label male reproductive organs (testes, sperm ducts, penis) and female reproductive organs (ovaries, oviducts, uterus)
Student can define fertilization and distinguish between internal and external fertilization with examples
Student can trace the development of a zygote into an embryo and its implantation in the uterus
Student can classify animals into oviparous and viviparous based on whether they lay eggs or give birth to young ones
visualIdeas: Schematic diagrams of the male and female human reproductive systems with key parts clearly labeled
An animation sequence showing a sperm cell fusing with an ovum to form a zygote (fertilization), followed by mitotic divisions forming an embryo
A visual timeline comparing development of a chick inside an egg shell (oviparous) versus a human fetus inside the womb (viviparous)

topics.title: Asexual Reproduction
objectives: Student can describe the process of budding in Hydra with a neat sequence diagram
Student can explain binary fission in Amoeba as a process of division of a single cell into two equal individuals
Student can state the significance of cloning and identify Dolly the sheep as the first cloned mammal
visualIdeas: A multi-stage sequence diagram of Hydra showing a tiny bulb-like projection (bud) growing, developing tentacles, and detaching from the parent
A sequence showing an Amoeba cell: nucleus elongating, dividing (karyokinesis), cytoplasm pinching (cytokinesis), and forming two daughter amoebae

topics.title: Adolescence and Puberty
objectives: Student can define adolescence as the period of life leading to reproductive maturity
Student can define puberty as the stage during which human bodies undergo changes to become capable of reproduction
visualIdeas: A human life stage timeline from infancy to childhood, highlighting the 11-19 age bracket as adolescence

topics.title: Changes at Puberty
objectives: Student can describe physical changes during puberty including sudden increase in height, changes in body shape, and voice change (Adam's apple)
Student can explain the increased activity of sweat and sebaceous glands leading to acne
visualIdeas: A line graph showing the rate of growth in height for boys and girls with age (9 to 18 years)
A diagram of the human throat showing the protruding larynx (Adam's apple) in a male adolescent

topics.title: Secondary Sexual Characters
objectives: Student can list the secondary sexual characters that distinguish males (facial hair, deep voice) from females (development of breasts, high voice)
Student can explain how secondary sexual characters are controlled by hormones (testosterone and estrogen)
visualIdeas: A comparison chart matching male and female secondary sexual characters along with the respective hormones driving them

topics.title: Role of Hormones in Initiating Reproductive Function
objectives: Student can trace the pathway of hormonal control from the pituitary gland to the testes/ovaries to release sex hormones into the bloodstream
Student can explain how endocrine glands release hormones directly into the blood to reach target sites
visualIdeas: A flow diagram showing: Pituitary Gland -> secretes hormones -> stimulates Testes/Ovaries -> release Testosterone/Estrogen -> reach Target Organs via blood -> trigger changes

topics.title: Reproductive Phase of Life in Humans
objectives: Student can describe the menstrual cycle including ovulation, thickening of uterine wall, menstruation, menarche, and menopause
Student can state the typical age range of the reproductive phase in human females
visualIdeas: A calendar-based sequence diagram illustrating the phases of a 28-day menstrual cycle showing uterine lining thickening and shedding

topics.title: How is the Sex of the Baby Determined?
objectives: Student can explain how sex chromosomes (X and Y) determine the sex of an unborn baby
Student can prove using a genetic cross why the father's sperm determines the sex of the child, dispelling the myth that mothers are responsible
visualIdeas: A genetic cross diagram showing female gametes (all X) and male gametes (X and Y) combining to produce XX (female) and XY (male) with 50% probability each

topics.title: Hormones other than Sex Hormones
objectives: Student can locate major endocrine glands on a human body outline (pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas)
Student can match endocrine glands with their hormones (thyroxine, adrenaline, insulin, growth hormone) and their corresponding target roles or deficiency diseases
visualIdeas: An outline of a human body with endocrine glands highlighted: brain (pituitary), neck (thyroid), kidneys (adrenals), stomach area (pancreas)
A quick matching table showing Thyroid -> Thyroxine -> Goitre, and Pancreas -> Insulin -> Diabetes

topics.title: Role of Hormones in Completing the Life History of Insects and Frogs
objectives: Student can state the role of insect hormones in insect metamorphosis
Student can explain the critical role of thyroxine and iodine in water for the metamorphosis of tadpoles into frogs
visualIdeas: A split cartoon of a tadpole growing in iodine-rich water (metamorphoses into a frog) versus iodine-deficient water (remains a giant tadpole, cannot mature)

topics.title: Reproductive Health
objectives: Student can list the key components of reproductive health: nutritional needs, personal hygiene, and physical exercise
Student can state the risks of adolescent pregnancy and explain the modes of transmission of HIV/AIDS
visualIdeas: A balanced diet plate tailored for adolescents containing iron, calcium, and proteins, next to a list of hygiene practices

topics.title: Force – A Push or a Pull
objectives: Student can define force in terms of a push or a pull acting on an object
Student can classify daily activities like opening a door, kicking a ball, and lifting a bucket as pushes or pulls
visualIdeas: Two panels: a person pushing a heavy cart with an arrow pointing forward, and a person pulling a drawer with an arrow pointing backward

topics.title: Forces are due to an Interaction
objectives: Student can explain how an interaction between at least two objects is necessary for a force to come into play
Student can predict what happens to objects in contact or proximity when there is no interaction
visualIdeas: A drawing of a man standing behind a stationary car (no movement), followed by the man pushing against the car (interaction and movement)

topics.title: Exploring Forces
objectives: Student can calculate the net force when two forces act on an object in the same direction
Student can calculate the net force when two forces act on an object in opposite directions
visualIdeas: An object with two arrows of 5N and 3N pointing right (Net = 8N to the right), and another with 5N right and 3N left (Net = 2N to the right)
A depiction of a tug-of-war where both teams pull with equal force, resulting in a net force of zero and no movement of the rope's center

topics.title: A Force can Change the State of Motion
objectives: Student can define state of motion of an object in terms of its speed and direction of movement
Student can explain how applying a force can increase speed, decrease speed, stop a moving object, or change its direction
visualIdeas: An animation sequence of a moving ball: a hand taps it in the direction of motion (speeds up), a hand blocks it (stops), or a hockey stick strikes it sideways (changes direction)

topics.title: Force can Change the Shape of an Object
objectives: Student can demonstrate how force can alter the shape of non-rigid objects
Student can list examples of shape changes due to force such as stretching a rubber band, pressing a lump of dough, or compressing a spring
visualIdeas: A series of small sketches: hands stretching a spring, a roller pressing dough on a board, and a finger pushing into a soft sponge

topics.title: Contact Forces
objectives: Student can define contact forces and classify muscular force and friction under this category
Student can explain how muscular force operates through physical contact and how friction always opposes motion
visualIdeas: An illustration of a bull pulling a cart (muscular force in contact) and a rolling ball slowing down on a rough floor with a friction arrow pointing backwards

topics.title: Non-contact Forces
objectives: Student can define non-contact forces and identify magnetic, electrostatic, and gravitational forces as examples
Student can describe how these forces act over a distance without physical contact
visualIdeas: A bar magnet attracting iron paper clips from a distance without touching them
A plastic comb rubbed with hair attracting small dry bits of paper (electrostatic force)
An apple falling vertically down from a tree branch (gravitational force)

topics.title: Pressure
objectives: Student can define pressure as force per unit area and state its formula as P = Force / Area
Student can explain why shoulder bags have broad straps and why a porter places a round piece of cloth on their head based on the area-pressure relationship
visualIdeas: A comparison of a sharp nail and a blunt nail being hammered, showing that the smaller area of the sharp tip concentrates force to yield higher pressure
A formula breakdown box showing that as Area (denominator) increases, Pressure decreases for the same Force

topics.title: Pressure Exerted by Liquids and Gases
objectives: Student can demonstrate that liquid pressure increases with depth and acts equally in all directions at a given depth
Student can show that gases also exert pressure on the walls of their container
visualIdeas: A tall plastic bottle filled with water, showing three water jets spewing from holes at different heights; the bottom-most jet shoots out the furthest due to maximum pressure
A drawing of a fully inflated balloon with arrows pointing outwards in all directions, representing gas pressure on the inner walls

topics.title: Atmospheric Pressure
objectives: Student can define atmosphere and atmospheric pressure
Student can explain the working of a rubber sucker in terms of atmospheric pressure difference
visualIdeas: A drawing of a rubber sucker pressed against a flat glass surface, with arrows showing external atmospheric pressure holding it in place
A cartoon showing a long column of air extending from the top of the atmosphere down to a person's head

topics.title: Force of Friction
objectives: Student can define the force of friction as a contact force that always opposes relative motion between two surfaces
Student can predict the direction of frictional force given the direction of an applied force
visualIdeas: A block being pushed to the right, with a large blue arrow showing 'Applied Force' and a smaller red arrow at the contact surface pointing left showing 'Frictional Force'

topics.title: Factors affecting Friction
objectives: Student can explain how surface roughness and interlocking of micro-irregularities cause friction
Student can differentiate between static friction, sliding friction, and rolling friction in terms of magnitude
visualIdeas: A highly magnified view of two flat surfaces in contact, revealing hills and valleys interlocking like teeth
A spring balance pulling a wooden block over a smooth glass sheet versus a rough sandpaper sheet, showing different force readings

topics.title: Friction : A Necessary Evil
objectives: Student can list three advantages of friction (walking, writing with a pen, stopping vehicles with brakes)
Student can list three disadvantages of friction (wear and tear of soles/tyres, heat generation in machinery, energy loss)
visualIdeas: A split screen showing: (A) a matchstick striking and catching fire (useful friction) and (B) worn-out soles of shoes and bald car tyres (harmful friction)

topics.title: Increasing and Reducing Friction
objectives: Student can state how grooving of tyres and treading of shoe soles increase grip/friction
Student can explain how lubricants (oil, grease, powder) reduce friction by forming a thin layer between surfaces
visualIdeas: A car tyre with deep tread grooves next to an athlete's spiked running shoe
A carrom board with talcum powder being sprinkled, showing a striker sliding much smoother across the surface

topics.title: Wheels Reduce Friction
objectives: Student can explain why rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction
Student can describe how ball bearings are used in ceiling fans and bicycles to replace sliding friction with rolling friction
visualIdeas: An illustration of a suitcase with tiny wheels being pulled effortlessly, compared to dragging a flat-bottomed suitcase
A detailed cutaway diagram of a ball bearing assembly showing metallic balls rolling between inner and outer rings

topics.title: Fluid Friction
objectives: Student can define fluid friction (drag) and list factors affecting it
Student can explain why airplanes, birds, and fish have streamlined body shapes
visualIdeas: A comparison of a modern airplane profile with the streamlined body of a bird in flight, showing smooth airflow lines wrapping around them

topics.title: Sound is Produced by a Vibrating Body
objectives: Student can define vibration as the rapid to-and-fro motion of an object
Student can identify the vibrating parts of musical instruments like the sitar, mridangam, and flute
visualIdeas: An illustration of a metallic school bell being struck, with wavy lines radiating outwards, and a finger touching the rim to feel the vibration
A table matching musical instruments (Sitar, Tabla, Flute) with their vibrating components (stretched string, stretched membrane, air column)

topics.title: Sound Produced by Humans
objectives: Student can locate the larynx (voice box) and explain how vocal cords vibrate to produce speech

Two children talking through a toy telephone made of paper cups and a stretched string, showing sound propagation through a solid

topics.title: We Hear Sound through Our Ears

topics.title: Amplitude, Time Period and Frequency of a Vibration

topics.title: Audible and Inaudible Sounds

topics.title: Noise and Music
objectives: Student can differentiate between noise (unpleasant, irregular sounds) and music (pleasing, regular periodic sounds)
Student can identify regular vs. erratic wave patterns on a sound visualizer
visualIdeas: A visual comparison of a smooth, regular sinusoidal wave (musical note) next to a highly jagged, chaotic and random waveform (construction noise)

topics.title: Noise Pollution

A list of remedial steps: planting trees along roads (noise buffers), installing silencers, and restricting loudspeaker hours

topics.title: Do Liquids Conduct Electricity?

A split-screen drawing showing the magnetic needle deflecting when dipped in salt water (good conductor) versus no deflection in pure distilled water (poor conductor)

topics.title: Chemical Effects of Electric Current
objectives: Student can describe the chemical changes that occur when an electric current passes through a conducting solution (gas bubbles, metal deposition, color changes)
Student can identify the gases evolved at the anode and cathode during the electrolysis of water
visualIdeas: A water electrolysis setup with carbon rods dipped in acidified water, connected to a battery, showing oxygen bubbles forming at the positive terminal (anode) and hydrogen bubbles at the negative terminal (cathode)

topics.title: Electroplating
objectives: Student can define electroplating as the process of depositing a layer of any desired metal on another material by means of electricity
Student can explain the movement of copper ions from a copper plate to a carbon/steel electrode in a copper sulphate bath
Student can list commercial applications of electroplating (chrome plating on bicycle handlebars, gold-plating on cheap jewellery)
visualIdeas: A detailed electroplating circuit showing a copper plate connected to the positive terminal of a battery and a brass key connected to the negative terminal, both submerged in a blue copper sulphate solution, with copper ions migrating to coat the key

topics.title: Lightning
objectives: Student can define lightning as a massive scale natural electrostatic discharge
Student can explain the historical discovery by Benjamin Franklin that sparks from clothing and lightning are the same phenomenon
visualIdeas: An illustration of Benjamin Franklin flying a kite in a thunderstorm to collect electric charge

topics.title: Charging by Rubbing
objectives: Student can explain how certain objects acquire electric charge when rubbed against specific materials
Student can demonstrate charge acquisition using a plastic refill rubbed with polythene or a balloon rubbed with wool
visualIdeas: A balloon being rubbed with a woolen cloth, showing static charge icons ('+' and '-') accumulating on the balloon surface

topics.title: Types of Charges and Their Interaction
objectives: Student can state that there are two types of charges: positive and negative
Student can formulate the law of electrostatics: like charges repel each other, and unlike charges attract each other
visualIdeas: Two inflated balloons rubbed with wool hanging near each other showing repulsion (arrows pointing away)
A charged balloon hanging near a charged plastic refill showing attraction (arrows pointing towards each other)

topics.title: Transfer of Charge
objectives: Student can build a simple gold-leaf electroscope to detect the presence of electric charge on a body
Student can define earthing as the process of transferring charge from a charged object to the earth
visualIdeas: A diagram of a home-made electroscope using a glass jar, a metal paperclip, and two small aluminium foil strips; when touched by a charged body, the foil strips diverge

topics.title: Story of Lightning
objectives: Student can explain the accumulation of positive charges at the upper edges of clouds and negative charges at the lower edges
Student can define lightning strike as the process of electric discharge between clouds and the earth
visualIdeas: A towering storm cloud with '+' charges accumulated at the top, '-' charges at the bottom, and induced '+' charges on the ground below, with a jagged lightning bolt connecting the '-' cloud base to a tree

topics.title: Lightning Safety
objectives: Student can list safe behaviors during a thunderstorm (staying indoors, avoiding open fields, crouching low)
Student can describe the design and function of a lightning conductor in protecting tall buildings from damage
visualIdeas: An outline of a tall building with a metallic lightning rod on top, connected via a thick copper strip down the side wall to a copper plate buried deep in the earth
A cartoon showing safe 'crouching' posture (head tucked between knees, hands on knees) for someone caught in the open

topics.title: Earthquakes
objectives: Student can define an earthquake and explain its cause due to the movement or collision of tectonic plates of the Earth's crust
Student can define the terms: seismic zones, focus, epicenter, seismograph, and Richter scale
Student can list three safety measures to protect oneself during an earthquake both indoors and outdoors
visualIdeas: A cross-section of the Earth showing tectonic plate boundaries sliding past or colliding, generating shockwaves
A diagram showing the Focus (origin point deep down), Epicenter (directly above on the surface), and concentric circles of seismic waves radiating outwards
A schematic of a seismograph showing a heavy pendulum with a pen trace on a rotating drum

topics.title: What makes Things Visible
objectives: Student can explain that objects become visible only when light from a source or reflected from the object enters our eyes
Student can differentiate between luminous and non-luminous objects
visualIdeas: A diagram showing a light ray traveling from a lightbulb, hitting a book (non-luminous), and reflecting into a human eye to show the pathway of sight

topics.title: Laws of Reflection
objectives: Student can identify the incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence, and angle of reflection on a ray diagram
Student can state the two laws of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and all three rays lie in the same plane
Student can define lateral inversion in a plane mirror
visualIdeas: A clean ray diagram of reflection off a flat mirror surface, with a dashed line for the normal, showing angle i = angle r
An illustration of a person standing in front of a plane mirror, raising their right hand while their mirror image raises its left hand (lateral inversion)

topics.title: Regular and Diffused Reflection
objectives: Student can compare regular reflection (smooth surface) and diffused/irregular reflection (rough surface)
Student can explain why diffused reflection does not mean the failure of the laws of reflection
visualIdeas: Parallel rays hitting a perfectly flat mirror and reflecting as parallel rays (regular)
Parallel rays hitting a bumpy, wavy surface and scattering in different directions, with normal drawn at each individual point to show angle i still equals angle r locally (diffused)

topics.title: Reflected Light Can be Reflected Again
objectives: Student can explain how multiple reflections are utilized in a periscope to view objects not in direct line of sight
Student can state the arrangement of mirrors in a barber's shop to see the back of the head
visualIdeas: A Z-shaped periscope tube showing two parallel plane mirrors fixed at 45-degree angles, tracing a light ray bouncing twice to reach the viewer's eye

topics.title: Multiple Images
objectives: Student can calculate the number of images formed when two plane mirrors are placed at specific angles to each other
Student can describe the construction and beautiful patterns formed in a kaleidoscope using three mirror strips
visualIdeas: Two mirrors placed at 90 degrees showing three images of an object placed between them
A three-dimensional cutaway of a triangular kaleidoscope tube containing mirrors and colorful broken glass pieces at one end

topics.title: Sunlight — White or Coloured
objectives: Student can define dispersion of light as the splitting of white light into its constituent colors
Student can describe a simple experiment using a glass prism or a water-and-mirror setup to demonstrate dispersion
visualIdeas: A narrow beam of white light entering a glass prism and fanning out into a rainbow spectrum (VIBGYOR) on the other side

topics.title: What is inside Our Eyes?
objectives: Student can draw and label the cross-section of a human eye including cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, and optic nerve
Student can explain the functions of the iris, pupil, rods, and cones in light regulation and image perception
Student can define blind spot as the junction of the optic nerve and the retina where no sensory cells exist
visualIdeas: A detailed, large cross-sectional diagram of the human eye ball with all major parts clearly labeled
An illustration showing the pupil dilating in dim light and constricting in bright light to control light entry

topics.title: Care of the Eyes
objectives: Student can list three healthy habits to prevent eye strain or damage (proper reading distance, avoiding looking directly at the sun, washing eyes with clean water)
Student can state the symptoms and cause of night blindness due to Vitamin A deficiency
visualIdeas: A comparison showing a student reading a book under low light at a bad angle vs. a student sitting straight in well-illuminated surroundings at a 25 cm reading distance

topics.title: Visually Impaired Persons Can Read and Write
objectives: Student can differentiate between optical aids (bifocal lenses, contact lenses) and non-optical aids (tactile, auditory, electronic aids) used by visually impaired persons
visualIdeas: A grid comparing non-optical aids such as tactile aids (Braillewriter) and auditory aids (audiobooks) with optical lens aids

topics.title: What is Braille System?
objectives: Student can describe the Braille system as a tactile writing system featuring raised dots in cells
Student can identify that the Braille system has 63 dot patterns representing letters, numbers, and punctuation marks
visualIdeas: A close-up of a Braille cell showing the 6-dot grid layout, with examples of patterns representing 'A', 'B', 'C' highlighted using raised red dots
